logs.diagnostics.suspect.exit1a: The command ran but hit a generic failure, so the real cause is usually in the command output just above this error.
logs.diagnostics.suspect.exit1b: A preceding build, packaging, or validation step may have failed before the wrapper command exited.
logs.diagnostics.suspect.exit126a: The target file or command exists, but it is not executable or the shell does not have permission to run it.
logs.diagnostics.suspect.exit126b: This can also happen when a script has the wrong interpreter or line endings.
logs.diagnostics.suspect.exit127a: The shell could not find the command in PATH.
logs.diagnostics.suspect.exit127b: A required tool may not be installed in this environment or the executable name may be wrong.
logs.diagnostics.suspect.exit130: The process was interrupted, usually by Ctrl+C or a cancelled terminal session.
logs.diagnostics.suspect.exit137: The process was killed abruptly, often because it ran out of memory or received SIGKILL.
logs.diagnostics.suspect.exit143: The process was terminated by SIGTERM, often because another process or supervisor stopped it.
logs.diagnostics.suspect.exitDefault: The exit code indicates the command failed, but the exact cause depends on the command output and environment.
logs.diagnostics.check.openLog: Open the linked log or full command output and look for the first error line above the exit code.
logs.diagnostics.check.rerun: Re-run the failing command by itself to separate wrapper failures from the real underlying issue.
logs.diagnostics.check.path: Check PATH and verify the missing executable is installed in this shell environment.
logs.diagnostics.check.permissions: Check file permissions, shebang, and whether the script needs chmod +x.
logs.diagnostics.check.shell: Confirm the command behaves the same in {{shell}}.
logs.diagnostics.suspect.macPackaging1: mac packaging commonly fails because of code-signing, notarization, or missing Apple certificate setup.
logs.diagnostics.suspect.macPackaging2: The Electron build may be missing an app icon, bundle metadata, or another required electron-builder config value.
logs.diagnostics.suspect.macPackaging3: A normal build step may have failed earlier, and the packaging wrapper is only surfacing the final exit code.
logs.diagnostics.suspect.build1: Compile-time failures such as TypeScript errors, unresolved imports, or environment-variable assumptions are common here.
logs.diagnostics.suspect.build2: A config file change may have broken the bundler, transpiler, or output path.
logs.diagnostics.suspect.npm1: The npm script may be failing inside package.json, so the root issue is often in the script it launches rather than npm itself.
logs.diagnostics.suspect.npm2: Node version mismatches, missing dependencies, or stale lockfile state can also surface as a plain exit code 1.
logs.diagnostics.suspect.shell: Shell scripts often fail because of missing execute permissions, bad relative paths, or an unexpected current working directory.
logs.diagnostics.suspect.python: Python command failures are often missing modules, the wrong virtual environment, or interpreter mismatches.
logs.diagnostics.suspect.signing: The error message already points at Apple signing/notarization as the likely cause.
logs.diagnostics.suspect.notFound: The shell output suggests a missing executable in PATH.
logs.diagnostics.check.macPackaging1: Check electron-builder config, app icons, signing settings, and whether the packaging step expects Apple credentials.
logs.diagnostics.check.macPackaging2: Look for the first packaging-related error line in the build output, not just the final npm failure.
logs.diagnostics.check.npm1: Open package.json and inspect the exact script behind this npm command.
logs.diagnostics.check.npm2: Try the underlying build or packaging command directly without npm to get a cleaner error.
